title: Python for Machine Learning
description: The core of the Python language: types, control flow, functions, iterators and generators, classes, errors and files, with examples from data processing and modeling.
overview: Python is the language of machine learning. The research code, the libraries (NumPy, PyTorch, scikit-learn) and most tutorials use it, not because it is fast, since it is not, but because it is quick to write, easy to read and glues together fast compiled code written in C, C++ and CUDA. A Python program is mostly orchestration: it describes the computation, and the libraries run it.

This chapter covers the parts of Python that machine learning code uses constantly: the built-in data types, functions, comprehensions, iterators and generators (the idea behind data loaders), classes (the idea behind models) and error handling. It assumes you have seen programming before. The next chapter turns to NumPy, where the real numerical work is done.
objectives: Use the built-in types (numbers, strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets) and explain mutability and aliasing.
Write functions with default and keyword arguments, and use comprehensions and lambdas.
Use iterators and generators to process data lazily, as in a mini-batch loader.
Define classes, including the fit/predict pattern for models, and use dataclasses.
Handle errors with exceptions, read and write files safely, and organize code into modules.

sections.title: Values, types and collections
body: Python variables are names that refer to objects, and objects carry their type. The basic types are integers (arbitrary size), floating-point numbers (64-bit), booleans, strings and the empty value None.

code: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3  # False! binary floating point (see Numerical Computing)

config.get('momentum', 0.9)  # 0.9: default if the key is missing

body: Assignment never copies an object; it makes another name for it. With a mutable object, a change through one name is visible through the other.

code: b = a            # b is another name for the same list
c = a.copy()     # a new, independent list (shallow copy)

body.warn: Aliasing causes subtle bugs in ML code: modifying a data array in place changes the original, and nested lists need copy.deepcopy. A common trap is a mutable default argument, def f(x, history=[]), where the same list is shared between all calls. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

sections.title: Control flow, functions and comprehensions
body: Blocks are defined by indentation. Conditionals use if/elif/else, and loops use for (over any iterable) and while.

code: """Unbiased sample variance of a list of numbers."""
body.caption: A function with a docstring. For [2, 4, 6] the mean is 4 and the sum of squares 8, so 8/2 = 4.0.

list: **Arguments** may have defaults and be passed by keyword: def train(lr=0.1, epochs=10) can be called as train(epochs=50). *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict.
Functions are objects: they can be passed to other functions and returned. A **lambda** is a small anonymous function, lambda x: x ** 2.
**Scope**: variables assigned inside a function are local. Reading a global is fine; assigning to one needs the global keyword, which is almost always a sign of bad design.
**Recursion**: a function can call itself. Python limits the depth (about 1000) and does no tail-call optimization, so prefer loops for deep recursion.

body: A **comprehension** builds a collection from an iterable in one expression. It is more compact and usually faster than appending in a loop.

code: evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]    # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
# Dot product with zip, which pairs up items
dot = sum(wi * xi for wi, xi in zip(w, x))      # 0.5 - 2.0 + 6.0 = 4.5
body.caption: List, dictionary and set comprehensions, and a generator expression inside sum.

body.tip: Useful built-ins: enumerate(xs) gives (index, item) pairs, zip(a, b) pairs items, sorted(xs, key=...) sorts by a key function, max, min, sum, any, all, and reversed. For numerical work, use NumPy instead of loops over lists (next chapter).

check.q: What does [x for x in range(10) if x % 3 == 0] produce?

sections.title: Iterators and generators
body: Suppose you need the squares of the first billion numbers, one at a time, to feed into a calculation. Building a list of a billion squares would fill the computer's memory. A generator is like a machine that hands you the next square only when you ask, remembering where it left off, so memory use stays tiny. The price is that you can only go forward, one item at a time. An **iterable** is anything a for loop can go through (lists, strings, files, ranges). An **iterator** produces the items one at a time and remembers its position. A **generator** is the easiest way to write an iterator: a function that uses yield instead of return. It computes each value only when asked, and so it is **lazy**: it can represent a huge or even infinite sequence in constant memory.

code: for start in range(0, len(xs), size):
for xb, yb in batches(xs, ys, 2):
body.caption: A mini-batch generator. The last batch is shorter.

body: This is exactly the idea behind the data loaders of deep learning libraries: a training set too big for memory is streamed in batches, and each batch is loaded, transformed and discarded. A generator expression, (f(x) for x in xs), is a comprehension that is lazy. Reading a file line by line with for line in f also never holds the whole file.

body.caption: An infinite generator, truncated with itertools.islice.

list: A generator can be consumed only once. Iterating again needs a new generator.
The itertools module offers building blocks: chain, cycle, islice, product, combinations, groupby.
Shuffling and batching, prefetching on a background thread and loading in parallel workers are layered on top of this same pattern.

check.q: The main advantage of a generator over building a list is that it
check.a: produces values lazily, using constant memory
wrong: runs faster in every case
can be indexed
can be iterated many times

sections.title: Classes and objects
body: A **class** bundles data (attributes) with the functions that operate on it (methods). The constructor __init__ sets up a new instance, and self refers to the instance. Machine learning libraries are built around this pattern: a model object holds its learned parameters and offers fit and predict methods.

code: """Least squares line y = a + b*x for one feature."""
sxy = sum((xi - x_mean) * (yi - y_mean) for xi, yi in zip(x, y))
sxx = sum((xi - x_mean) ** 2 for xi in x)
return [self.intercept + self.slope * xi for xi in x]
body.caption: A model with the fit/predict interface. The data (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5) give the line y = 1/3 + 1.5x of the Linear Regression chapter.

list: **Special methods** (double underscores) let objects behave like built-ins: __len__ for len(obj), __getitem__ for obj[i], __call__ to call an object as a function (a neural-network layer is a callable object), __repr__ for printing.

**Inheritance**: class Child(Parent) reuses and overrides the parent's methods. Neural-network libraries have a base Module class that your layers extend. Prefer **composition** (an object that holds other objects) to deep inheritance hierarchies.
A **dataclass** generates the boilerplate for classes that only store data: it writes __init__, __repr__ and equality from the annotated fields.

check.q: In a method definition def fit(self, x, y), self is
check.a: the instance on which the method is called
wrong: the class itself
the first training example
a keyword that must not be used

sections.title: Errors, files and modules
body: When something goes wrong at run time Python raises an **exception**. Unhandled, it stops the program with a traceback that names the failing line. Handle the exceptions you can recover from, and let the others stop the program.

code: raise KeyError('config needs a learning rate')

body: A **context manager** (the with statement) guarantees cleanup: the file is closed even if an error occurs.

code: rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))           # list of dicts, one per row
body.caption: Reading a CSV file into dictionaries and writing JSON. Libraries such as pandas do the same in one call.

list: A **module** is a .py file; import it with import module or from module import name. A **package** is a folder of modules. The standard library (math, random, statistics, collections, itertools, json, csv, pathlib) covers a lot before any installation.
Use a **virtual environment** per project (python -m venv .venv) and pin library versions, so that results can be reproduced (see Software Practice).
A **decorator** wraps a function to add behavior: @functools.lru_cache caches results, @dataclass transforms a class, and @torch.no_grad() disables gradient tracking.
**Type hints** (def f(x: float) -> float) document intent and let tools catch errors; Python does not enforce them at run time.
if __name__ == '__main__': lets a file work both as an importable module and as a script.

body.note: Python is slow for loops over numbers: the interpreter does bookkeeping for every operation. A pure Python loop summing a million numbers takes roughly 50 milliseconds, while NumPy takes about one. Numerical code therefore uses vectorized array operations (next chapter), and the Python layer only coordinates them. Use the timeit module or a profiler to find where time is actually spent before optimizing.

check.q: What is the main benefit of opening a file with a with statement?
check.a: The file is closed automatically, even if an error occurs
wrong: The file is read faster
The file is loaded into memory entirely
Errors in the file are ignored

quiz.q: What does -7 // 2 evaluate to in Python?
quiz.why: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4. Rounding toward zero would give -3, which is what some other languages do.

quiz.q: A grid-search script wants to store a result under the key (lr, batch_size), for example (0.1, 32). Which of these can serve as a dictionary key?
wrong: the list [0.1, 32]
the set {0.1, 32}
the dictionary {'lr': 0.1, 'batch': 32}
quiz.why: Dictionary keys must be immutable so the hash table can find them again; a tuple is immutable while lists, sets and dictionaries are not.

quiz.q: After a = [1, 2]; b = a; b = b + [3], what is a?
quiz.why: The expression b + [3] builds a new list and rebinds the name b to it; the list that a refers to is never changed. Only a method like b.append(3) would have changed it in place.

quiz.q: A word counter runs counts = {}, then for each word w executes counts[w] += 1. What happens on the very first word?
quiz.a: A KeyError is raised, because the key does not exist yet
wrong: counts[w] is created with the value 1
counts[w] is created with the value 0 and then incremented
Nothing happens until w is seen a second time
quiz.why: Reading a missing key raises KeyError. The pattern counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1 supplies a default for the first occurrence.

quiz.q: Given def f(a, *args, **kw): return len(args) + len(kw), what does f(1, 2, 3, x=4) return?
quiz.why: The extra positional values 2 and 3 land in the tuple args, and x=4 lands in the dictionary kw, giving 2 + 1 = 3. The first positional value 1 is bound to a.

quiz.q: What does [x * y for x, y in zip([1, 2, 3], [4, 5])] produce?
wrong: an error, because the lengths differ
quiz.why: zip stops at the shortest input, so only the pairs (1, 4) and (2, 5) are formed. Pairing every item with every other item would need a nested loop.

quiz.q: total = 0, then def add(x): total += x, then add(5) is called. What happens?
quiz.a: An error, because total becomes a local variable that is read before it is set
wrong: The global total becomes 5, because += updates the variable that already exists
total stays 0 and no error occurs, since the function only changes a copy
A new global variable total is created holding 5 the first time the function runs
quiz.why: Any assignment inside a function creates a local name, so the increment tries to read a local that does not exist. Updating the global would need the global keyword, which is usually a design smell.

quiz.q: g = (x * x for x in range(4)), then print(sum(g), sum(g)). What is printed?
quiz.why: The squares 0, 1, 4, 9 sum to 14, but the generator is used up by the first sum, so the second sum sees nothing and returns 0.

quiz.q: A batching generator slices a list with xs[start:start + size] for start in range(0, len(xs), size). With 10 items and size 4, what are the batch lengths?
quiz.why: The starts are 0, 4 and 8. Slicing past the end is allowed, so the last batch simply holds the 2 remaining items.

quiz.q: A training set is 200 GB but the machine has 16 GB of memory. Why does a generator-based data loader still work?
quiz.a: It keeps only the current batch in memory and discards it before producing the next
wrong: It compresses the dataset so that it fits in 16 GB
It loads the whole dataset once and then reuses it from the cache for every epoch
It reads the data faster than a list could, so memory use stops mattering for large files
quiz.why: A generator is lazy: each batch is produced on demand and then released. Memory use depends on the batch size, not the dataset size, though the data can only be read forward.

quiz.q: Why does list(fibonacci()) never finish when fibonacci contains while True: yield a, but list(islice(fibonacci(), 8)) does?
quiz.a: The generator is infinite, and islice stops after 8 items
wrong: A generator can be turned into a list only through islice
yield pauses the function, and list cannot resume a paused function
islice computes the sequence in a faster, vectorized way
quiz.why: list keeps asking for items until the iterator is exhausted, which an infinite generator never is. islice takes a bounded number of items and then stops asking.

quiz.q: A neural-network layer object is applied as layer(x), as if it were a function. Which special method makes that possible?
wrong: __getitem__
__init__
__repr__
quiz.why: __call__ lets an instance be called like a function. __init__ runs only when the object is created, and __getitem__ handles indexing such as layer[0].

quiz.q: With a dataclass TrainConfig that has fields lr = 0.1 and epochs = 20, what does TrainConfig() == TrainConfig() evaluate to?
wrong: False, because they are two different objects
An error, because equality is not defined
True only if the objects are the same one in memory
quiz.why: A dataclass generates __eq__ from its fields, so two instances with equal field values compare equal. Without the decorator, the default comparison would be identity and give False.

quiz.q: After SimpleLinearRegression().fit([0, 2, 4], [1, 2, 6]), what is the fitted slope?
quiz.why: The means are 2 and 3, so Sxy = (-2)(-2) + 0 + (2)(3) = 10 and Sxx = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8, and the slope is 10/8 = 1.25. The intercept is 3 - 1.25 × 2 = 0.5.

quiz.q: def safe_divide(a, b) wraps return a / b in try with only an except ZeroDivisionError clause. What does safe_divide(1, 'x') do?
quiz.a: It raises a TypeError, since only ZeroDivisionError is caught
wrong: It returns nan, since the handler catches every kind of error
It returns None, since the try block did not finish
It raises a ZeroDivisionError from the failed division
quiz.why: An except clause catches only the exception type it names. Dividing by a string raises a different error, which propagates and stops the program.

quiz.q: Given def double(x: int) -> int: return x * 2, what does double('ab') do?
quiz.a: Returns 'abab'; type hints are not enforced
wrong: Raises a TypeError before the body runs, because x is not an int
Converts the string to an integer first and then fails
Returns None, since the argument type does not match the hint
quiz.why: Hints document intent and help external tools find errors, but the interpreter does not enforce them. Here the body happens to work on strings, since repetition by 2 is valid.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the line if __name__ == '__main__': in a Python file?
quiz.a: It runs only when the file is executed directly, not when it is imported
wrong: It makes the file importable as a module
It declares the function that Python must call first in every program
It prevents other files from running the code
quiz.why: When imported, __name__ is the module's name rather than '__main__', so the guarded block is skipped. A file is importable regardless of this line.

quiz.q: Summing a million numbers takes about 50 ms with a pure Python loop and about 1 ms with NumPy. What explains the gap?
quiz.a: The interpreter does bookkeeping on every operation; NumPy runs one compiled loop
wrong: NumPy uses a smarter algorithm that needs far fewer additions than the loop does
Python integers are stored with fewer bits than NumPy uses, which slows each add
NumPy skips the memory transfers that the Python loop would need
quiz.why: Both perform about a million additions; the difference is the overhead per operation in the interpreter. NumPy hands the whole array to compiled code, which is why numerical Python is vectorized.

summary: Names refer to objects. Lists, dicts and sets are mutable, so aliasing matters: copy when you need independence. Strings and tuples are immutable.
Functions take positional, default, keyword, *args and **kwargs parameters. Comprehensions build collections concisely; zip, enumerate and sorted cover most loops.
Generators yield values lazily, which is the model of data loaders that stream batches from disk.
Classes bundle state and methods. The fit/predict object is the standard model interface; dataclasses hold configuration; special methods like __call__ make objects behave like functions.
Handle errors with try/except, use with for files, organize code in modules and virtual environments. Python is slow for numerical loops, which motivates NumPy.

q: Why does this function have a bug, and how would you fix it?
solution: The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and is shared by every call that omits the argument: add_item(1) and then add_item(2) returns [1, 2] the second time. Fix:
problems.a: The mutable default argument is shared between calls; use None and create the list inside.
